eminent in less than two months. We are now in the eighth month of this fiscal year, and nearly all the money voted has been voted without much discussion. It is so near the end of the year that we could not consider properly the estimates presented. Why are we in this position? First, because this house was called together late last spring when there was only one month before the life of parliament was to end. Then it was called late this year with only three months before the Christmas holiday.
We are expected to finish work in three months that ordinarily ought to take six months. I suggest that it is asking too much of parliament to do all that work and do it well in that short time. All this without mature consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I readily

Now I come to another point. Before the house votes further supply to this government I think we should have a clarification of certain principles stated by the Acting Prime Minister from his place here yesterday. He stated some principles that I think we should discuss. The issue, it seems to me, is clearly drawn. It is simply this: Which shall prevail, the will of a ministry which has grown autocratic, or the will of the elected1 representatives of the people? This government, without, in my judgment, a shadow of justification, relies on a mere technicality and attempts to deny to the duly elected representatives of the people the right, which they have to investigate every aspect of public affairs. On this issue the decision should not be Left in doubt. [DOT] Yesterday, in an attempt to justify the1 government's position, the Acting Prime Minister enunciated some of the most extraordinary constitutional principles which have been heard in this chamber since confederation. Stung by public criticism from coast to coast of his refusal to allow the representatives of the people to examine all orders in council passed while parliament has been in session, he pronounced certain autocratic principles which have not been heard in any democratic chamber in the last century. He took issue with two statements which I had made on a previous occasion. I will repeat them. I said-Hansard, October 31, 1945, page 1681:
It is a vital principle, which no member will dare to challenge, that this House of Commons has the full and inalienable right to a disclosure of all actions of the executive. It has the right and the duty to review and pass upon all such actions.

The other statement to which he took exception is as follows:
For so long as I hold this seat I am determined to ensure, in so far as lies within my . power, that Canada is governed by this House ' of Commons, by the elected representatives of the Canadian people, and not by the secret diplomacy of the council chamber.
I do not retreat, Mr. Speaker, one single step from the position which I then took. That position is sound and that principle must triumph if responsible government is to prevail in Canada.
Tor a person allegedly espousing Liberal principles, the Acting Prime Minister's suggestion that all authority of the cabinet is received from the crown and not from the House of Commons is to me incomprehensible. However right he may be technically, in actual fact that principle is as dead as Queen Anne. I never expected to live to see the day when a man holding the office of Acting Prime Minister in a Liberal government in Canada would attempt to resurrect it; and I have no hesitation in saying to this house that the Acting Prime Minister's attitude yesterday was a betrayal of much that Liberalism in Canada claims to stand for.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How do you know?

I wonder what the old Liberal guard of this house, those that have drunk deeply at the springs of Liberal principles, thought of that attitude. How those words yesterday must baffle and bewilder one of the great crusaders for the supremacy of parliament-the Prime Minister himself. The Acting Prime Minister's words must have come to him as a greater shock than the atomic bomb whose control he is at present discussing.

When he learns of those statements of the Acting Prime Minister, the Prime Minister's mind will assuredly turn back to the shades of Wilkes and Pym and Hampden-yes, and to the shades of William Lyon Mackenzie and Louis Joseph Papineau, sturdy rebels who stood out against this kind of doctrine in our land.
When I am addressing these words to a Liberal administration I am on sound ground. speechtext: You can't even make the grade.

Had I the time I could find in Hansard scores, yes, hundreds of statements from the lips of the Prime Minister. Listen to these words of his; I quote now from Hansard of 1920, volume 1, page 31. These are his words:
Mr. Speaker,-	.

-there should be an end to government by order in council.

During the war, government by order in council may have been necessary and may have been tolerated to a large extent by the people; but the time has now come when, if we are to have government in the true sense of the word, that government must be by parliament and through parliament; it must not be by the substitution of the diplomacy of cabinet councils, carried on by cabinet ministers in their secret chambers, for the free discussions and questionings of the ministry in this house in regard to public affairs.

Where is that citadel to-day? Can this parliament be styled the citadel of freedom when it is denied even its elementary rights, and denied them with petulance and bad temper?
Later in the same year the Prime Minister had this to say-Hansard, June 30, 1920, page 4540:
X think the time has come when there should be an end to monopoly of control of the affairs of Canada by a cabinet carrying on the country's business in secret councils.
That is from the leader of the hon. member who sits opposite. I continue:
The business of the country should be carried on in the Open on the floor of this parliament in such a manner that the government will be obliged to take into their confidence not only the members of parliament, but the people of the country whose money they are voting to expend.
There, Mr. Speaker, exactly stated, is the principle for which I contend in this house to-day; there is the principle for which I will not cease to contend.
In the session of 1921, tire voice of the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime, Minister, was again raised. This time the question was directly that of accounting for expenditure of public moneys, the identical problem which presents itself to us to-day. On that occasion what did he say?
Why did he have to say t?
For fellows like you.

Why do I have to say it to-day? This is what he said'-Hansard, 1921, page 1292:
Let me say to my right hon. friend and to his government that the people of Canada will hold him and his government accountable for every cent of public money whether it is expended directly by the minister in charge ol a department, or by any corporation or other creature 'which the ministry itself may create foi the purpose of carrying on its business. . . .

Hear, hear.

I am glad to see that hon. members opposite support these views. Down through the years similar statements were made by the right hon. gentleman to whom the Acting Prime Minister owes allegiance, but whose views he apparently disregards.
I shall quote only one further statement. Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne on January 29, 1934, the then leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister of Canada, had this to say:

-rather than an executive which derives its powers from and is responsible to the House of Commons.
The Acting Prime Minister yesterday said:
The authority of the government is not delegated by -the House of Commons; the authority ot the government is received from the crown.

Indeed, the House of Commons has come to be, in the phrase used by ,the Prime Minister himself not so l-ong ago, a sort of rubber stamp for what -the ministry may choose to do, regardless of how its own wishes and desires may be expressed and regardless of how much -those wishes and desires may represent the wishes and desires of the people at large.
Perhaps the Prime Minister's absence, instead of making his finance minister's heart grow fonder, has operated on the -basis of "out of sight, out of mind." They are -those upon which the whole Liberal party stood in the election of 1935 when this government was first elected to office. To this end it would repeal the legislation enacted by the present administration, which deprives parliament of its control over expenditures and taxation and invests the executive with unwarranted, arbitrary powers, as for example: 1. legislation permitting the executive to enact measures by order in council for peace, order and good government: and 2, legislation providing the executive with a "blank cheque" for expenditure of this kind.
A good many measures, Mr. Speaker, that have been passed this year by this house have been blank cheques. I could produce many other authorities, the words of many other leaders, but I have confined myself to the words of the right hon. gentleman who leads this government, believing that hon. gentlemen opposite would be more prepared to take into sympathetic consideration words which fell from his lips and which I have quoted.
I repeat, the issue is clear. This parliament is a democratic institution or it is not. If this administration has nothing to hide, then let it be frank and open with the representatives of the people. In view of the statements made yesterday I thought it was necessary that these comments be made. With respect to the measure now moved by the Minister of Finance, let me say that I ask only one question. How much time is the government going to allocate for the discussion of these estimates before parliament prorogues?

We
have been reminded this afternoon that time is precious. I am going to be brief because I believe that example is better than precept.

My opinion is, and I expressed it yesterday, that it is time the house itself, and not merely the government, took responsibility for the delay in considering the public business of the country. There is a sentence in one of the speeches of the Prime Minister read to us this afternoon, which says that the power of the executive is derived from the House of Commons. Power of the executive may be said to be derived from the House of Commons in one sense. That sense is this, that at all times the government must see that it possesses the confidence of the House of Commons, otherwise it must retire from office. I stated that yesterday; I stated it as emphatically as I could. No one in modern times would ever have the temerity to say anything else. If hon. gentlemen will read my remarks of yesterday from beginning to end they will see that I made it most clear, I think repeatedly so, that the government is responsible to parliament and that the House of Commons at all times has the power, by an expression of its voice, to withdraw its confidence from the government, in which event the government has to resign. Everything I said yesterday was constitutionally correct. It was technically correct, and it was in spirit correct. The contention of the leader of the C.C.F. party that the constitution has changed since the British North America Act was passed with regard to the source of the powers of the executive is unwarranted.

I said it was a fiction written into the act.
Mr. ILS'LEY: It is not a fiction. The section of the British North America Act which I quoted was this:

The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the queen.
That is, in the crown. The words "the queen" are not used in any personal sense; and any talk about the queen having been dead for forty or fifty years is entirely irrelevant. .The crown is a continuing entity. The crown is the head of the executive of Canada. The members of the cabinet of Canada, the government of Canada, are the crown's advisers, sworn in as members of His Majesty's privy council, and they derive their authority from the act. But as I have said, they must, at all times, be able to command a majority in this House of Commons. In that way the House of Commons has a control over His Majesty's advisers which it can exercise at any time.
I said yesterday the duties of this House of Commons were three. The first is to control expenditure. Listening to the leader of the Progressive Conservative party this afternoon one would think that yesterday I had combatted' the contention that it was the function and duty of the House of Commons to control expenditures. Why, Mr. Speaker, that is its primary function; it is one of its main functions.

There is no point of order,

to force the production of confidential and privileged documents, stated so to be by His Majesty's advisers.
One would think from the1 quotations read from the speeches by the Prime Minister that the position taken by this party and by the Prime Minister had1 been that all orders in council could be produced); that blanket orders for the production of executive acts of His Majesty's advisers should be agreed to. My hon. friends will search Hansard in vain to find a motion by the Prime Minister for the production of all orders in council passed between certain dates. Om the contrary in 1926, and again in 1936, he very properly took the position that orders of that kind could1 not and should not be passed by the house. While he was in opposition-and he was not very many years in opposition-he never took the position that there should be this attempt to force out into the open confidential documents on a blanket basis; there is not one request for them by the Prime Minister.
Then, the second function of the1 House of Commons-and I referred to it yesterday -is the voting of supply. That is the reason I am here to-day with this motion. I am here to have supply voted. The House of Commons may refuse to vote supply. The power of refusing to vote supply is a power over the executive which tihe House of Commons has, which nobody can deny, which nobody would wish to deny, which nobody would dare to deny.
I understand this afternoon interim supply is to be voted, and that there is no objection to the voting of supply. But certainly anyone who would take the position, or would represent me as taking the position, that in some way we can get money without the House of Commons, is taking a position which cannot in any way be supported.
The third function of the House of Commons is the enactment of legislation. We are here to enact legislation. I wish now to refer to what I said yesterday at the conclusion of my remarks after the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had spoken. I said:
Section 9 of the British North America Act reads:
"The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the queen."
And section 10:
"The provisions of this act referring to the governor general extend and apply to the governor general for the time being of Canada-" 47696-132 .
And from there on the section was not relevant, and I did not quote it. Then I said:	-
The authority of the government is not delegated by the house.
Does anybody here say that authority is delegated by the house? Never in any of the Prime Minister's speeches does he say authority is delegated by the house.
His Majesty's advisers a-Q. sworn in as advisers to the crown. The government is responsible to parliament, which I have admitted in every word of my speech, but that is a different thing from the doctrine that the government is a committee of the House of Commons or that it exercises authority delegated by the House of Commons. That is not so.
I stand by every word I said yesterday. I consider myself as good a Liberal as, and a lot better Liberal than, the leader of the opposition although he was a Liberal for a long time. I have nothing to apologize for in that regard.
If the conduct of the executive does not appeal to the House of Commons, then as I said yesterday-and wish to say again'-we have made fuller disclosure than has been made in any other parliament I remember or of which I have learned. We put everything that we can with safety put before the House of Commons.
Oh, oh.

And when I talk about "safety" I am using the language as Bourinot used it-honour and safety; safety to the public interest.
If the opposition feel that our conduct in any of these respects is irresponsible or reprehensible, then they have their remedy, by moving a vote of want of confidence in the government. Let them go ahead and do so, if they want to. I am reminded of an historical remark attributed to Charles II- "They will never kill me to make James king."

Mr. Speaker, the motion of the Minister of Finance is that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. I object to the system we are now following in this house. A civil war was fought in Great Britain for more than two hundred years to secure for parliament control over expenditures.
Here we are in the thirteenth day of November; the year is nearly out, and yet not one dollar of civil estimates has been voted in committee of supply. Here we are near the end of November; money has been spent, and

Housing Act

we are simply conducting a post mortem. We are asked to spend nearly four billions of dollars a year of the taxpayers' money, with no sympathy whatever for the man who pays the taxes. Are not we who sit in parliament to have some of our rights and privileges restored to us, or has parliament surrendered its functions and powers and rights to the executive? I have complained about this time and again.
Order. The hon. member for Broadview has the floor and there should be order in the chamber.

I have great sympathy for the Minister of Finance but I also have sympathy with the taxpayers.
If I could have a little order in the chamber, Mr. Speaker, I would be able to continue.
For many years I liiave been a member of the House of Commons and have represented my constituency. I do not expect courtesies or favours from the government-far from it. I am here to watch and to preserve and to maintain the rights of private members to have some check over expenditures.
As I have said, I have sympathy with the Minister of Finance, realizing something of the heavy burdens he is carrying. But I have sympathies, too, for many others back home in the constituencies who are paying the piper and carrying the burden of taxation, one which is reacting heavily upon the poor man and the returned soldier.
Instead of parliament having control over expenditures, and instead of government of the people, by the people and for the people, what have we now? We have government by order in council and by dollar-a-year men. We have, government'by control boards which are spending money like water.
I have been objecting along these lines for a long time. As recently as September 11 of this year I asked about the action being taken by the auditor general. Where is the auditor general? He has no power to veto many of these expenditures, but he should have. On September 11, at a time when the house had been sitting only three or four days, I said, at page 69 of Hansard:
Ait the present time we have virtually no control. All kinds of bodies, over the head ot parliament, are spending money like water. Every principle for which the British nation struggled in the old land since the seventeenth century has been surrendered to the political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxss shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
1 want to emphasize to the committee that powers of legislation older even than the right ox taxpayers to determine the national expendi-

ture have been surrendered, and if we are to
continue this sort of thing the power of parliament will be gone forever. Whole spheres of activity, involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country, have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law and of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal..
X do object, now that the war is over, to the way that business is being conducted over the head of parliament. We are told that parliament is supreme. That is only a myth. If parliament is supreme, why has it not now control over these outside bodies a'nd their expenditures and in the result we will only hold a post mortem as the money is spent.
I object to this vote. I support what my leader has said, and I reaffirm what I said on September 11. I protest that we are spending four billion dollars over the head of parliament, over the head of the taxpayers. For nearly a hundred years the executive have been the servants of the House of Commons; they have been also the servants of the taxpayers who pay the money. We had the War Measures Act, and now that the war is over we are to have a new War Measures Act. With these controls it is impossible for our business men, large or small, to conduct, their business. I do object to our being asked to vote supply, until the middle of December of $29 million more. The sooner we regain our rights, the better it will be. Parliament should have the absolute control of all expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $29,769,000.11, being one-twelfth of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March. 1946, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, be granted to His Majesty on account for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1946.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
intend to indulge in any controversial matters, my intention being to make some constructive suggestions with regard to the curtailment of expenditures. As I have said repeatedly since the beginning of the session, there is no use talking in the abstract; we must come down to brass tacks. We must find ways and means to reduce expenditures. This might prove a difficult problem if handled improperly, but if hon. members rolled up their sleeves and decided to start to work they might accomplish something.
The only way is to secure charts of the various departments to find out if each branch in the department is of any use to the state.

Housing Act
If a branch is found to be of no use, it should be abolished. If a branch is found to be useful, each civil servant in that branch should be considered on the basis of his usefulness to the state. If his work is nod useful, the only thing to do is to tell him that he has outlived his usefulness. '
The elimination of useless branches or dead branches would represent a lot of money in each case. These branches should be given the benefit of the doubt, but when a branch is found to be useless it should be abolished. When a man in a department is receiving dominion pay for work which is not of any use to the government, he should be fired. By this method we can reduce the load of taxation now upon the shoulders of the Canadian people. It is the only way to do it. The public accounts committee is in session and members are trying to unearth scandals. They may succeed in that, but what will be the benefit? It will be nil.
V hat should be done by members of parliament is to consider the civil service as something that should be improved. I was the chairman of the civil service committee for one session and afterward I wms a member of the committee under the able chairmanship of the present Minister of Public Works. For the first time in the history of parliament I attempted to consider the civil service in relation to its usefulness to the state. They were all scandalized. When I would complain of someone, hon. members would rise and tell me that the man was an honest civil servant.
Then I received visitors. Although I applied the padlock law t.n my room, the lady visitors whom I received were homely rather than comely; they were not good looking at all. They were complaining because nature had not been generous to them, because the fairies had not touched their cradles with their magic wands. I remember one who seemed to be very bright but she was not the kind of girl that the big stores of New York would use in the spring or the fall to display their new clothes. She said, "You know it is unfortunate; I know I am not good looking but I think I have some brains; I do the work of a stenographer grade three and I receive the pay of a clerk grade one; on the other hand, there is a beautiful girl jivith bleached hair who does not even do the work of a clerk grade one and she is paid as a stenographer grade three." She was the receptionist for the boss. I told her that we should have this corrected by the civil service commission. I wrote to the commission and an investigator from the organization branch went to the department and asked the boss 47696-132J
what work this grade three stenographer was doing. The boss said that she was splendid. Of course, she was, but not for her work. Then he asked about the girl who was doing nearly all the work in the branch but who was not as good looking as the other one. He said, "Oh, that poor girl, we keep -her here for charity's sake." The only report made by the investigator was based on the rvord of thfe boss.
" It is unfortunate, but it is impossible to reform the civil service. I will not believe anyone or I will not listen to anyone who is not ready to make a direct suggestion, particularly in connection with any reform. At the end of last wreek I met a former cabinet minister. He told me that as soon as he was sworn in he met his colleagues around the table-this happened quite a long time ago -and they were all told to curtail useless
^ expenditures in their departments. This man was earnest and he said, "I will do that." He returned to his department and checked up and found sixteen who had nothing to do, and he fired them-. "The result," he said, "was as if the sky had fallen down on my head. N-obody else had fired anybody. I was the only one who had ever fired sixteen, and they still blame me for that although it happened a very long time ago."
I said the other day, and I repeat now, that it will take a lot of courage to reform the civil service, because whenever you desire to fire someone who is incompetent, a crowd of friends gather around to tell you: Do not make a fool of yourself, for that man is a good man. Or. as was said to me at the sittings of the civil service committee, he is an honest civil servant. I remember a girl-I never met her. but Dorothy was her name-who had been unsuccessful nine times in passing her examination. Her father was a constable in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. She was not put on a blacklist. She was still kept on in the office, working there. When I saw her record I asked an official of the civil service commission. "Is it possible to keep on a girl who knows absolutely nothing and is absolutely incompetent?" The civil service commission took action and the girl was fired, and who protested on her behalf? Her chief officer, who said that it would be most unfortunate to fire this voung girl because she was most useful in the office. I leave it to you to decide whether she- was pretty or not-I never met her. That is what happened in that case.
Injustices are most frequent in the civil service. What we have to do is to go with a w'ell-sbarpened axe into all the departments and bring about reform by cutting off all the
Housing Act

dead branches. In these times state charity is substituted for private charity. Private charity did marvels before the war. How is it possible for any member of parliament to do what he could do before the war now that we have so much taxation bearing down upon our shoulders? It is useless just to protest against taxation if we do not take steps to curtail useless expenditure to the rock bottom. And the only way to do that is to cut down useless expenditure in the civil service here in Ottawa and outside. That is the only way.
What happens, for example, in the Department of National Defence? I have been told that at a restaurant in town a C.W.A.C. captain met someone from the National Defence office who was not exactly a brass hat but used to wear a red tab oh his lapel. She said to him, "How is it that you are in civvies to-day?" He answeredf

and this has probably been brought about by the strong denunciations of my friend the hon. member for Fraser Valley-"Well, we are most unpopular as brass bats, so now we have to dress in civvies." The thing to do, and some day I will do it-I will do it on the estimates-is to show what a -lot of useless branches were established by the brass hats under Ralston and McNaughton, and which are .the curse of the Department of National Defence. They have psychiatrists teaching nonsense to the fellows who are there-psychiatrists who are just as crazy as the deputy minister of health himself. They are positively crazy- and we have to pay for them.
When we go home we have to consider expenditures. Why? Because a large proportion of our indemnity is taken away from us in taxes. And why taxes? Taxes to pay for parasites. Is there a member of parliament who would be willing, if there were no taxation on our indemnity cheques to sign cheques for the maintenance of parasites in the Department of National Defence, or any other department here in Ottawa? Would the Minister of National Defence, if there were no taxation to maintain them', be ready to pay the same amount for the maintenance of those people as he is forced to contribute from his indemnity and his salary to-day for their maintenance? And because it is the state that pays them, is that any better. Is it any more logical that we should maintain these parasites just because the state pays them? Canada is the garden of Eden for all those who won't work. It is not necessary to work to have consideration in the public service. That is not important at all. The work of a man or woman in the civil service does not count at all. That is immaterial.

What is important is the staff. Let me illustrate. Suppose that Tom has a staff of one or two men. or girls who work hard and do their work very well, are conscientious and ' useful to the state. They will be ten times less considered than the man who has a staff of thirty girls who knit around him and twenty boys who play chess or arrange their moustaches or chew gum around him. What is essential is the staff, and the larger the staff the more consideration and the more pay. Some people will scream about what I am sajung now. They will say it is blasphemous. But they do not realize that the Canadian people are fed up with bureaucracy. And we cannot get any information from these people. I am a Liberal and I am a radical.
There are big branches that are useless. As I have said in previous years, one of the first branches I would abolish would be a big one; it would be the Bank of Canada. That would mean a big saving to the people of Canada. I should like to have ministerial responsibility restored in the person of the Minister of Finance. I remember the times of Jim Robb. He was just a plain-clothes business man like the member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew). He was a man of common sense. He did not have to stand up to defend all these bureaucrats who were brought here by R. B. Bennett and who were supported by those two nefarious men, Charlie Dunning and Ralston-and I know what I am talking about. I remember the time when the Bank of Canada was organized, and when a man named Osborne was brought over from England to organize it along the same lines as the Bank of England. Before that our banking system in Canada was very good. Why should be have a Bank of Canada here with Graham Towers in charge as a despot, receiving twice the salary of the Prime Minister of Canada?-and it is impossible to get any information about his travelling expenses, bonuses and so forth. The minister will not deny it. I remember very well complaining in the time of Charlie Dunning of a doorman there. I do not. remember his name, but he always wore a Prince Albert, which seemed silly. He was brought here by Bennett as his valet. I asked what amount was paid to him, and if it was paid from the dominion exchequer. I could not get any answer. Mr. Bennett was very indignant: he said, how could a member ask a question like that about the Bank of Canada? The Prime Minister said the- same thing; he could not understand why I was so indiscreet as to want to know whether it was the state or R. B. Bennett who had paid for the trip of that doorman to Australia or

Housing Act
some other place in the antipodes. And we have reached that point: it is a secret of state. Well, just as well dispense with all that and save the people's money.
Besides that, I complain of the fact that Graham Towers is considered omniscient- not only omnipotent but omniscient. He will be on the housing scheme. The country could not live without Graham Towers. How is it that it prospered before he was born? It is the same thing with the deputy minister of finance, a man whom - I have denounced time and time again, and it was a privilege to denounce him. All these fellows are dangerous, because they are bringing the country to ruin. I can say that, now that the victory loan is over and it has been oversubscribed-and I am very glad. I would not have dared to speak like that before the victory loan was over, because everybody would have said that I am a traitor. But now we can consider business, and I wonder whether members of parliament are ready to put a stop to all this over-expenditure, and go and make a clean-up in the civil service commission-and not only in the civil service commission, for these are minor offenders, but go to the "big bugs", go to the "high-ups" and see what they are doing and what is their usefulness to the state. What will be the answer of the minister, or anybody else in the party? He will say, they are great Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I thought so. I knew he would do that. Although I am not a mind reader, it has been told me so often that I am accustomed to it. I know what is going on there. Are we not great Canadians? But I will suffer; it is not we who receive $35,000 a year. We work; we are the shock absorbers for the policies of the government; we are shock absorbers for all those notions drafted by these cranks and imposed on us, and we have not the right to criticize them. Well, well, that is enough!
At a meeting on behalf of the victory loan I said that I would be a watch-dog of the treasury in the house. How 'is it that the Russians are laughed at because of the icons which they have almost all over their walls? Here we have icons which are much more costly than those one might have found encrusted with jewels in Russian houses during the old Czarist regime.
I shall be called unfair. I shall be called unpatriotic. I shall be called dumb. I shall be told that I have not enough intelligence to understand the great services these people are rendering to this country. I shall be told
all that. Perhaps those who will tell me that will be right. I am very modest when I am called a lunatic, because I say to myself, perhaps he is one who calls me one, and therefore there is no use arguing with him.
But now, sir, we are told to do something. What has to be done must be done in committee, and it must be done in the private offices if hon. members want to cheek expenditures. They will have to examine the reports of the departments, but they should also have charts of all departments and of the Bank of Canada. They should mark the connection of the Bank of Canada with the Bank of England and with the Bank of International Settlements of Basle, Switzerland, and concern themselves about the man who is in charge there. One of our colleagues once referred to him as a Jew. The question is not whether that man is a Jew, a French Canadian, a Roman Catholic or a Mohammedan. That is not the point. The point is that that man was chosen by Sir Otto Nie-meyer, of ill fame, as well as Montagu Norman, at the time that the representatives of Great Britain were meeting German representatives during the war at the Bank of International Settlements at Basle. A long time ago Vespasian said that money has no odour. We may say that too, because money runs from us and we see so little of it that we can hardly smell it. But those gangsters of international finance-Montagu Norman, Niemeyer, Rasminsky here in Ottawa, are all alike; they are dangerous.
Hear, hear.

I hear my friends of the Social Credit group say "hear hear". I appreciate it. But I regret very much that when I was alone in denouncing Dunning and Ralston in this chamber, while the hon. member for Lethbridge said "hear hear" he never supported me by naming those who should have been called' by. name. Get rid of them.
At the present time, sir, I will not move anything; I know that my .motion would be defeated. But I express the wish to all hon. members, from the acting leader of the government down to the humblest member-who is myself-that all members of parliament join in undertaking constructive reform for the welfare of the country at large. I wonder whether members of parliament would, be ready to t?.ke the charts of all departments, and study them, and examine as to what is the usefulness, of each branch and what is the usefulness of each civil servant or dominion employee who works in it.
In 1938 the seas were very high at the sittings of the parliamentary committee on the civil
Interim Supply

service; a.t times navigation was most difficult. But fifteen days before the report came I notified the Liberal caucus that we would have a unanimous report. We had it. The main recommendation of that report was to have a standing civil service committee of the House of Commons. There is a similar committee for the senate; it has not been sitting lately, and. I do not wish to put the blame on the senate or anyone else; but the fact is that that committee has not held any sittings. There should be a committee of the house with which any civil servant could lodge his complaint without any fear of his superior officer. That proposal was carried unanimously. The following year, under the chairmanship of the Minister of Public Works, the same committee came out with the same recommendation. That recommendation, if adopted, would have had a very good effect on the relations between civil servants and their chiefs, but it was not adopted. It was held fon a time, because of the war, we were told. But now, after V-E day and V-J day, I would suggest to the government that the proposal be put into effect and that the rules be amended- by abolishing, for instance, the useless debates committee, of which I have been chairman for many years, which has never sat, and which was never instructed to sit, and having a standing committee on the civil service. Then members from the different parties and groups could meet together to protect long-suffering civil servants and do something to eradicate parasites from the civil service, thereby saving money to the Canadian taxpayer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not supposed this resolution would be debated to auy great extent. I personally had not intended to make any remarks until the committee was set up. I believe I am to be one of the members of that committee, and I had decided to reserve what I have to say until the committee commences its work. But during the discussion the other afternoon on this resolution to set up a committee in connection with a Canadian flag certain remarks were made which I believe should not go unanswered. I refer particularly to the speech made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose). I recognize that the hon. member has a right to speak in this house, having been duly elected by his constituents. I feel thankful that we live in a democracy with free speech, so that in this parliament my hon. friend is able to say the things that are upon his heart. That is one privilege our democratic system gives to every member of parliament. I do not think I would have taken so much notice of what the hon. gentleman said if he had said it as a private

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I intend to read once more the resolution that is before the house:
Resolved, that in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that Canada possess a distinctive national flag and that a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to consider and report upon a suitable design for such a flag.
As far as that resolution is concerned, it consists of two parts: first, a declaration that it is expedient that Canada possess a distinctive national flag, and second, that a committee be appointed to consider and report upon a suitable design for such a flag.
I intend to discuss this resolution this afternoon as dispassionately as it was discussed by the minister when he introduced .it. There is no subject on which one could speak that gives greater opportunities for exalted expression of sentiments than the flag. The hon. member who preceded me made eloquent reference to the union jack and suggested that it should have >a prominent place in any national flag that should be designed for Canada. I express those Same sentiments. One hundred and fifty years ago on my father's side my ancestors came to this country in order to seek freedom under the union jack. My maternal ancestors

Canadian Flag
came to the Red river as Selkirk settlers. They came to this country which had as its emblem the union jack.
I am not going into a discussion to-day on the merits or demerits of other viewpoints. But after listening to the minister making the speech he did the other day, in well-chosen and restrained language, it seemed to me he indicated that he believed that the red ensign should be declared officially what it has been unofficially before, the flag of this dominion; for he stated that the red ensign was accepted officially as Canada's national flag from confederation to about 1904; it had been Canada's official flag abroad since 1924; it was flown, he said, at the Quebec conference; it was flown as well at San Francisco; and finally, on September 5 of this year, by an order in council, provision was made that it should be flown over these parliament buildings until such time as a national flag should be decided upon.
There have been motions on this subject on previous occasions. Various motions were made by Mr. Cameron McIntosh, who on more than one occasion said that if a national flag were chosen for Canada the union jack should have a prominent place on that flag. Then in 1938 Mr. Dickie, a Conservative member, moved the resolution to which the minister made reference in his address, that in the opinion of this house a national flag representing the Dominion of Canada should be adopted, and that in any design for a Canadian flag the union jack must be conspicuous. That, therefore, was the viewpoint not only of a Liberal but also of a Conservative.
In my opinion, sir, any flag which is determined upon for Canada must embody two ideas: one, Canada as a nation with a distinctive flag; the other, Canada within the empire.
When some contend that to preserve the union jack would preserve an emblem of conquest, let me tell them that rather is it the emblem of freedom and tolerance which has brought millions of people from all parts of the world to Canada to seek freedom under its folds.
May I also point out that South Africa has had her experience in this respect. South Africa's white population divided as between the Dutch and the English. In 1927, debate took place in the house of assembly in South Africa which it would be well for hon. members to read and ponder. I spent several hours reading the debates in the South African house of assembly. On the one hand was General Hertzog, then the prime minister, whose attitude was that any flag for South Africa should have no reference to the union jack because it would be emblematic of conquest. On the other hand was- General, now
Field Marshal. Jan Christian Smuts, whose attitude was that there was no suggestion of conquest in the acceptance of the union jack He said:
If anyone says after what has happened at the imperial conference and the acceptance by the people of this country of what has been done there, that the union jack means the superiority or dominion of one race, I" fail to follow that, or to see the logic of that statement.
That was the attitude of that great leader of empire. His views were opposed by Hertzog, who in unmeasured language condemned all who would have the union jack upon the flag of South Africa.
I do not think it is necessary to discuss to-day whether Canada should have a national flag. There are those who say that'it means separation from the empire. When I was at the Olympic games in 1936, one thing which impressed me was that, regardless of what Canada's position might be in those games, I was never able to determine where Canada was in any of the races, because we had no flag. The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, now Viscount Bennett, of whom no one can say that he lacks faith in or love of this country or love of the empire, said in 1938:
Upon the large question I expressed an opinion in the house some years ago that I believed it was desirable, as I do to-night, that the country should have some flag by which it can distinguish itself from other parts of the world.
I cannot see eve-to-eye with those who say we must not have a national flag. On the other hand I cannot see eye-to-eye-and my sentiments so carry me that I must be restrained when I say this-with those who would deny the union jack a permanent and a prominent place on the flag of this country; and the place of honour on any flag is the upper quarter. I stand to-day where Mr. Bennett stood in 1938. I do not deny to any group in parliament the authority, but I challenge their right, considering the need of maintaining our unity to father a flag which, in omitting the union jack, will disrupt and divide this dominion. Some say, why not compromise? I will compromise on anything, but, speaking for myself, not to the extent of the removal of the union jack from our national flag.
When Cameron McIntosh introduced his resolution from year to year, he asked that- ... a special select committee be appointed for the purpose of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian, flag, representing Canada as a whole, thereby-	.
And I accentuate these words:
-symbolizing the dominion senior partner in the British commonwealth of nations.
Canadian Flag

Having said that much, I come to a specific question, and generally in regard to the pledge which was given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the Canadian Legion some time prior to August last. I noticed, when the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) the other night read what the Prime Minister said, that some in the house did not applaud it. The Prime Minister, according to the Legionary, said this:
It would be unthinkable to have a flag for this dominion that did not contain the union jack.
And he-
. . . assured the legion officers that, so far as he was concerned, the new Canadian flag should certainly contain the union jack.
A year ago, on August 11, 1944, during the debate on foreign affairs only two speakers took part. Most considerately-and I have always found it so-this house gave me an opportunity to speak on foreign affairs; the Prime Minister set aside on hoar to give me that opportunity; and on that occasion I advocated what I had advocated both in 1940 and for twenty-five years, namely, that we should have an unhyphenated Canadian nationality based not on racial origin but on service to this country in war and in peace. That was my idea of citizenship, and the Prime Minister on that occasion said that he would undertake at the earliest possible moment to introduce a bill into parliament in order to ensure the principles of Canadian nationality which, I may add, though accepted in the past in theory, were never accepted in fact. Then he said, at page 6276 of Hansard of August 11, 1944:
And not only do I wish to see our people recognized as Canadians, but I also wish to see a Canadian flag recognized in this country. I would like to see the flag that our Canadian men are fighting under to-day. We have a Canadian flag unfurled in battle to-day by our very brave men in Italy and in France. I think in time the people of this country of Canada wil say we want to have as a Canadian flag the flag they are carrying in battle to-day.
That is what he said in 1944, and according to the minister that flag was the red ensign; for at page 1935 of Hansard of November 8 of this year, he said:
On October 22, 1943, the cabinet war committee agreed that the army should provide for flying the Canadian red ensign where Canadian forces were serving with forces of other nations.
So that when an amendment was moved by hon. members on this side of the house the other day, the idea behind it was that instead of putting this matter into the cockpit of a committee where there may be engendered passions such as resulted from the

placing of a similar question in committee in South Africa, we suggested that the government face the issue as a government and by a bill in that behalf officialize the non-official red ensign, which- has been accepted as our flag since 1867. That is why we did that. If you read the debates in South Africa with General Hertzog and General Smuts on opposite sides of the question, you will have revealed the bitterness that was engendered. I ask this parliament therefore, with all the force at my command, to be careful about the submission of a matter such as this to a committee. We have been restrained in our language here; but there I am fearful that instead of the cause of Canadian unity being advanced it will be in fact retarded.
If the Prime Minister were here I would ask him specifically one simple question: Will you give us your solemn pledge that, regardless of what recommendation may come out of the committee, the flag which will be made official for Canada will have the union jack in a prominent place? The minister, in his excellent speech, went so far as to leave one with the impression that three or four more words would have completed that speech with an expression on his part that apparently he felt that the red ensign, the Canadian red ensign, should be made official.
I am going to ask the Acting Prime Minister, in whose name the resolution stands, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who brought it to the attention of the house and explained its purport, to give us an answer on this very important question, an answer which I believe is demanded all over the dominion to-day by the men and women who served in the armed forces in two wars, and by the vast majority of the people scattered across Canada-the answer that the union jack will have the prominent place. They are fearful; they are anxious; they are asking us in this parliament not to do anything at this time which will in any way cause any division between our people.
I believe in compromise. Many take the view that only the union jack should be the flag; we say, "No, we will go with you in the interests of Canadian unity. We will have a Canadian national flag. But we are asking, when we compromise, that we be not asked to give away that portion of the flag on which our people came to this country to seek freedom and liberty."

speechtext:
Before the six
o'clock recess, Mr. Speaker, I had discussed the first part of the resolution, which states that in the opinion of this house it is expedient that Canada possess a distinctive national flag. I do not intend to carry on any further discussion in regard to that portion of the resolution. I have already placed before the house the question I asked of the government, the answer to which would do much to allay a feeling that is to-diay in the hearts of many people in this country, namely that, having regard to the large number of designs for a new Canadian flag, this committee might very well arrive at a conclusion and recommend to this house a flag design upon which the union jack does not appear. On the part of the opposition we take a very strong stand on this question. We do not believe we deserve the criticism so often leveled against us, that we still regard Canada's position as colonial. That is not our attitude. Far from it. Our attitude is that at a time when we are beginning to realize more and more the necessity of the maintenance of the empire connection in the interests of our survival, in cooperation with the United States and our other allies, certainly is no time when a message should go out from any committee of this parliament or otherwise that we are going to permit the removal or the ostracism of the union jack from the national flag.
I know that view is shared by many hon. members, some on the other side of the house. I was quite amazed to hear the remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) the other da}'. I wish he were in the house
at the moment, so that if I misinterpret him he might correct my interpretation. If I understood him aright, however, having regard to his proposals for the discontinuance of appeals to the privy council, for the power to amend our own constitution, and finally for the establishment in Canada of a distinctive flag, I took from his words that his party stood for the establishment of a national flag upon which the union jack would not appear.

Now', Mr. Speaker, I have said what I intended to say in that regard, and I do not think I will carry that controversy any farther. However, I hope the leader of the C.C.F. party will make his stand clear, because it is impossible for anyone reading his speech intelligently to come to an}' conclusion but that in his speech the other day he meant to imply that as far as his party was concerned it intended to dissociate itself from requiring the union jack to be * on the Canadian flag.
I now pass on to the next portion of the resolution, which has to do with the setting up of a committee to recommend designs. I pointed out this afternoon what happened in South Africa when a similar course was followed. As far as population is concerned South Africa is in a similar position to Canada. The government of that country first set up a committee of the assembly with a view to determining a design. So acrimonious were <he debates in that committee that no report was presented, and the matter was concluded at the end of that session. Then a commission was set up, but for some reason that commission was unable to come to any final or generally acceptable conclusion. Finally the government of that country, under the premiership of General Hertzog, brought in a design for a flag under legislation which was
[Mr. Maclnnis.3
known as the South African nationality and flag bill. What they actually did was to combine a measure analogous to the citizenship bill now before this house with the flag bill. Anyone reading the reports of that committee can only conclude how devastating to national unity in the country were the debates and discussions which took place in the committee. Excepting the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), other hon. members have received many designs, and in the debate we have heard many different opinions. We heard the opinion of the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot), which was definite and clear; we heard the opinion of the leader of the C.C.F., which the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) states was definite, and which I state was far from clear. We on this side have our opinion. There are still others with different opinions.
I ask you, sir, what is going to happen if this matter is submitted to a committee, into which will be channeled and tunneled suggestions and designs from all over the country? In my opinion out of that committee, if ever agreement should come-and for the life of me I cannot see how agreement could ever come- would come, at the best, a bizarre and hybrid design.

Does anyone expect that in that committee there will be a higher degree of unanimity than there is in the house among members in various parts of this chamber? I think General Smuts summed the matter up very well when he said that if the matter were left to a committee there would be difficulties, separation and division, with consequent ill-feeling and that, finally, the committee might 'bring to the -house a flag which would be acceptable to few if any members. On that occasion he said:
If you mutilate flags, you lacerate people's feelings, and in the end you alienate all sympathy from the flag which you establish in that way.
In South Africa the matter was sent to a committee where it was debated for several days. Then it came back to the house of assembly, and the bitterness of debate in that assembly has never been exceeded by that of any debate on any issue in the history of the Canadian House of Commons. Finally, out of all this-first a committee, then a commission, then a committee, then a submission of designs to a committee, and finally a bill submitted to the ass'embly, and -by the assembly resubmitted to the committee-came this result: by statute it is provided, not that -the Union of South

Canadian Flag
Africa should have a flag, but that the Union of South Africa shall have two flags. The statute reads as follows:
The flag of the union shall be
(a)	The union jack to denote the association of the Union with the other members of the group of nations constituting the British commonwealth of nations; and
(b)	The national flag of which the design is set out in section 8.
Then the statute goes on to state how they are to be flown. It states:
The union jack shall be flown with the national flag from the houses of parliament and from the principal government buildings in capitals of the union and of the provinces, at the union ports, and on government offices aoroad, and at such other places in the union as the government may determine.
The result is that South Africa has two official flags flying side by side.

They should have some instruction from parliament in session, setting before them the aim and ideal expected )f them. Otherwise, as I said before, out of this committee-provided the necessary majority could be secured for the purpose-might very well come a recommendation for a national flag which would in no way contain the union jack in a prominent place.
The other dav an amendment was moved and, for reasons which vour Honour knows, that amendment was declared ineffective. Since that time I have had an opportunity of studying the amendment proposed in the assembly of South Africa by General Smuts. So that this parliament will be assured that, whatever design is arrived at by the committee, the House of Commons will know that the national flag evolved will have thereon the union jack occupying a prominent place in the upper left-hand corner. I move, seconded by the hon. member for High Park (Air. McMaster) :

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): In spite of the fact that- the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated a desire to have some expression of opinion or speech from the government, I am not rising at this time to speak in the name of the government. The resolution that is before us is, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, something which should1 be lifted above the plane of partisan politics. This is not a matter of the government or of the opposition. I submit to you, sir, that it is the desire of a great many hon. members of this house to act as Canadians on this question.
We are not asking the house to choose a flag for a party. We are asking that there be chosen a flag for the Canadian people, a flag of the Canadian nation, and I have more confidence in the members of this house who will be designated to form the committee to select an appropriate design than has been implied in many of the speeches we have heard since this motion was brought forward.
I do not wish to make any odious comparisons, but I do not think what may have happened1 years ago in South Africa is a sufficient rock or shoal to deter this nation from setting out upon the course which appeals to the majority as being the proper one. I had hoped, when the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) completed his speech in support of the resolution, that very little more would be said on this matter at this time. It seemed to me that what he had said fairly represented what I hoped would be the feeling on the matter of the majority of those who are interested in this question. Let me remind hon. members of some of the things which he said. For instance:
We in Canada have shared the union jack, and we shall always honour it as the symbol of much that is best and most precious in our heritage.
Canadian Flag

I do not think any member of this honourable house would quarrel with that statement. The union jack is a symbol which represents much that is best in the heritage of all those who derive their traditions and their culture from western Europe. The three colours of the union jack are the three colours under which the whole of western Europe marched, fought and bled from the crusades onward, and the crosses that are now part of the union jack represent much of what we in Canada, from whatever race we spring, all honour as precious and good in our heritage.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) pointed out the other day that the white field was the flag carried by William the Conqueror from Normandy to the British isles. The red cross on that white field, the Cross of St. George, was the cross which the English crusaders brought back from an expedition from which I think most of the members of this house derive some pride because of the purpose on which those noble crusaders were bent at that time. That was their way of expressing the ideals prompted by the generous impulses of their nature. And when the Cross of St. Andrew on the blue field reached Scotland it was brought there, according to my recollection of history as I learned it, by members of the Bruce family, also from Normandy; and the Cross of St. Andrew was joined with the Cross of St. George on the same field. The Cros3 of St. Patrick, a white cross-I believe it was originally a golden cross that replaced the harp on the banner of that isle -was joined1 .with the others-the white Cross of St. Patrick with the similar diagonal Cross of St. Andrew with, superimposed upon them, the Cross of St. George.
From what we learned many years ago, the blue was the blue of the mantle of St. Martin, carried for the first time as a relic, a sacred standard to inspire the troops of Clovis and afterwards of Charles the Great. The red had the same religious origin. It was taken from the mantle or tunic of St. Denis. These colours, were the colours associated with the Christian civilization as it developed1 in western Europe.
I do not believe that any of us in this country at this time regard the union jack as oeing a symbol of conquest or a symbol of subjugation. It is under the union jack that the institutions of this Canadian nation have grown and developed and have brought us to the point where now, and for a good many years now, the dominion is and has been an autonomous state subject in no phase of its domestic or of its external affairs to any other

authority than this Canadian parliament.
The minister added:
But we have had nothing that has been peculiarly and indisputably our own, that would symbolize Canada-all of Canada and everyone in Canada. There should be something that all can see and look to with pride, as -the symbol of this great nation of ours, to^ which affection and loyalty can -attach, and which can become the sign of the unity and purpose that will make Canada great.
The minister did not stop there. Lest there be any possibility of misconstruction of those words he went on to say:
In advocating that Canada have a flag of its own, we are not suggesting that a narrow nationalism become our goal. Far from it. We are not turning our backs on the British commonwealth; far from it. We are not drawing away from the new international community of the united nations; far from it. It is the firm intention of -the government, and of everyone in Canada, that we shall continue to play our part in the British commonwealth, an association of nations that has been an example to the world.
May I interject the hope that this example may be followed by the nations of the world. If it is, I think we shall have reason to be happy and proud of the organization so recently set up. The minister went on:
It is equally our intention that Canada shall be a strong and unselfish voice, and a courageous and active member in the united nations; that is our hope for future peace. All of that is our purpose. In our laudable l-onging to have a national flag we are only seeking to give to the spirit of Canada, -to the enthusiasm of our people and to the sacrifice of our men in two terrible wars, the symbolism t-ha-t all other-nations have joined to create a force in their national life, the symbolism of a national flag.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in those words with which any hon. member can disagree, and that is all the first part of this resolution asks this house to express:	"That in the opinion of this house it
is expedient that Canada possess a distinctive national flag." I hope that can be unanimously accepted by the members of this house. The resolution then goes on to suggest that a committee of members of this house be appointed to join with members from the other place to choose a proper design for such a flag. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) cited the other day what had been expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as his own feeling in the matter, and I think the words can well bear repetition:
Mr. King assured the legion officers that, so far as he was concerned, the new Canadian- flag should certainly contain -the union jack. It might be debatable whether a single maple leaf in the fly would be preferable to -the Canadian coat of arms at present incorporated in* the Canadian red ensign, but it would be unthinkable to have a flag for this dominion -that did not contain the union jack.

Canadian Flag
I have not been here very long, but I have been a good many years in Canada; and my experience has been that there are a good many people in Canada who usually share the views of the Prime Minister. It has not been his experience to find himself in any small minority upon Canadian affairs. If a committee is chosen to select a suitable design for a flag that will be a distinctive national flag for Canada, I would be very much surprised and, I may add, disappointed if a.majority of that committee did not have the same feeling about it that the Prime Minister expressed in his declaration to this delegation from the legion.
The purpose for which it is suggested there should be a distinctive national flag is, I think, a laudable one; 'to have a symbol that all Canadians can look upon as distinctively their own, not because they want to discard the union jack, but because the union jack is not distinctively their own and because they feel that their nation has now reached the stature in t'he family of nations that requires it to have something which can be regarded as its own. Whether that would be accomplished by the coat of arms in the fly of the Canadian ensign or whether a single maple leaf in the fly would not be preferable is something which may be debatable. The object of this resolution is not to give instructions to a committee but to select a committee representative of all groups in the house to act with members selected from the other house to choose a suitable design. Of course the coat of arms is distinctively Canadian; but I do not think there are many who do not regard the maple leaf as something typically Canadian, and consideration might very well be given to the question as to whether of not the maple leaf is not something that would be at the same time simple, appealing and distinctively Canadian.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs said to you, Mr. Speaker, that he had ideas of his own about what would be a proper design. So has each of us; but so also have a great many people who are not members of this house. I am told that a great many designs have been prepared by Canadians; good Canadians; Canadians anxious to do something for their country; Canadians anxious to be of some service in having selected and adopted a distinctive symbol that can serve as a rallying point for all Canadians. It seems to me it is not going too far to give those Canadians this little mark of consideration, that at least the work they have done, the sincere desire they have exhibited to produce something, should receive the courtesy of being looked at by the members of the committee, of being passed
upon and some consideration being given to the sincere, patriotic feelings of those who took the trouble to prepare and forward something for submission. I think that would be small thanks to them for the patriotic motives which have prompted them to go to such pains. If I might be permitted, without being regarded as impertinent, I should like to voice here my own thanks to each and everyone who went to the trouble of thinking of this problem, of giving it some consideration and of putting forth something which he, though he may be alone, felt would be of service to his fellow Canadian citizens.
When all that is done I do not anticipate in that committee the acrimonious debates or discussions that have been looked upon as possible. I would imagine the temper of that committee would be pretty much the temper of the Canadian people. The Canadian people can be roused when there aire those who set out to rouse them, but when they are asked to consider calmly what is in their interest and in the interests of their fellow Canadians they usually come to a pretty fair and reasonable conclusion. I remember predictions made even in this house as to what would happen to me when I went back to Quebec East. But I was able to meet the people of Quebec East, and to say to them that had they known what I knew I was convinced that they would have done as I did. And I got a pretty fair response from them. '
So far as I am concerned, on this motion I am prepared to say now that I for one fully share the views expressed by the Prime Minister to this delegation of legionairies, but that I have sufficient confidence in those of my fellows in the house who will be chosen to serve on the committee to allow them to consider the question and to bring in a recommendation. I am not committing myself -as to what I shall do when their recommendation comes in. But at this time I have sufficient advance confidence in, them to feel that they can be trusted to examine the question, and to bring to the house a recommendation which I hope and! trust will have such an appeal for the great majority of Canadians that it can receive the seal of approval of this house, and hereafter serve as the symbol to which the minister referred in these closing words of his speech, as something:
The children of to-day and, let us pray, the children of to-morrow will strive for and gain a new peace, a new freedom and a new security under the protection of the flag of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for just a few moments to complete the record on a vital point that was made by two members of the house, the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Kidd) in an able presentation and the hon. member'.for Grey North (Mr. Case) in a colourful speech. Both made the point that this government did not have a mandate to deal with this question of the flag. I am to-night going to follow the leadership that was given to-day by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and use the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for my text. This is what he had to say in a speech delivered in the city of Winnipeg on a significant day, May 24, 1945, a speech which received wide publicity:
Another of the symbols we lack is a distinctive national flag. We have a flag-a distinctive flag-which has long been used on our merchant ships at sea. It is the flag which is flown at international conferences and over Canadian diplomatic missions abroad. But, what is of the greatest significance for us to-day, it is the flag which our Canadian troops carried into aattle. It is the flag under whose folds great areas of Europe were liberated. That flag is the Canadian Red Ensign.
At my suggestion, the government directed that, in honour of our lighting men, the red ensign should be flown from the Peace Tower of the. parliament buildings at Ottawa from sunrise on V-E day to sunset on the following Sunday which was the day of thanksgiving for victory. That recognition has, I believe, been greatly appreciated throughout Canada.
I recall all this because I believe the time has come when Canada, like Australia, like New Zealand and like South Africa, should have a distinctive national flag. The need for a distinctive flag is all the greater when we reflect that the Canadian troops who are to serve against Japan are to serve with the forces of the United States. They will wish to carry into battle in the orient the flag they have fought under in Europe.
We shall, of course, always honour the union jack as the symbol of the British commonwealth and empire. What Canada's distinctive national flag should be, what its design should be is, I
 '
believe, a matter which the people themselves, through their representatives in parliament should decide. I feel, however, the decision is one that should not be delayed. May I, therefore, say at once that if on June 11, the present government is continued in office, and I am myself still a member of the House of Commons, 1 shall, at the first session of the next parliament, ask parliament to approve and authorize a distinctive Canadian flag.
I need not point out that the election did take place on June 11, with results that are well known to the country and to the members of the house, and in pursuance of that mandate we find this in the speech from the throne, at page 8 of Hansard of September 6, 1945:
My ministers believe that the position attained by our country among the nations of the world, makes it desirable that Canada, like the other nations of the British commonwealth, should possess a distinctive national flag. You will be asked to appoint a select committee of members oi both bouses of parliament to consider a suitable design for a Canadian flag.
The government has directed that, pending approval by parliament of a particular design, the Canadian red ensign which was the flag carried into battle by the Canadian army, and which was flown from the peace tower on V-E day and V-J day as a tribute to the valour of our armed forces and to Canada's achievements in war, may be displayed wherever place or occasion makes it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the record.
I should like to say that I belong to the "red duster" school because the union jack has peculiar and important significance to me. I want to preserve it. I want to incorporate it in whatever flag we have, for I remember very well that Canadian men and women served for six solid years under the "red duster," fought under it and died under it, and to-day in plots which are forever Canadian, in Britain, in France, in Belgium, in Holland, in Sicily, in Italy and in North Africa they sleep under it in eternal peace. Along with thousands of mv comrades I want to remember them as I left them in those eventful days and nights when we parted company. I want to recall the plots, the rows of crosses and the inscriptions, the quiet countryside and the flowers and the "red duster" flying overhead, proclaiming to all people that these are Canadians.
To this house may I say: let parliamentarians speak; let committees meet. The deed is done; the decision. I believe, has been made; and in good time that which they wanted will become our decision.
