speechtext:
In speaking of the maritime provinces, it would be well for us in this country to remember a little of the history of Canada. In 1713 the treaty of Utrecht was signed. Under that treaty, from Acadia were constituted the three provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and part of Maine, Labrador and
Newfoundland also came under the union jack. So that we are the first part of Canada which can claim to have been under the union jack, and the part of Canada which has been under it the longest. We should also remember that, some years before confederation was even considered in other parts of Canada, it was in the little island down by the sea-the garden of the gulf, as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) would say-that the question of confederation of this great country was first conceived. The seed was there sown, and I believe that the great country which Canada is to-day is due to a great extent to the deliberations which were carried on at that time. So that Canada owes much to the maritime provinces.
If I had time I could point out many other matters for which Canada owes a great debt to our maritime provinces. I should particularly like to point out, as was mentioned this evening by one hon. member, that after and during the American war of independence thousand and tens of thousands of peopje in what were then the Thirteen Colonies left that country-for what purpose? That they might live under the union jack. They came to my own province of New Brunswick; and the city of Saint John-what is known as the "loyalist city" and the first incorporated city in British North America-was built by the United Empire Loyalists. So that we have a lot of history back of our relations with Canada and supporting our desire to see the union jack an important feature of our Canadian flag.
I might also point out many other reasons. During the last war no part of Canada gave, in proportion to population, more men to the Canadian forces than did the maritime provinces. The same thing was true in this war. I might also point out what the ports of Halifax and Saint John have done during this war and the last. Further, so far as victory loans are concerned the maritime provinces have done their share and more than their share. I was quite pleased this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Prince Edwards Lennox (Mr. Tustin) boast of what his constituency had done during the last victory loan. It deserves great credit. Last week, I believe, an hon. member mentioned that he thought his constituency was one of the first in Canada to reach its quota. But I would point out that five days after the victory campaign was opened, the county of Charlotte, New Brunswick, not only reached its quota but exceeded it 'by 136 per cent. I understand that to be a record, not only for New Brunswick but for all Canada, and I know that the
Canadian Flag

hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), had he had an opportunity, would have mentioned it.
As far as a flag is concerned, I have not been against all change. I feel that we in this country need a distinctive flag; I have felt that for a good many years. I remember that during .the last war I happened to be in London on armistice day, and saw there the flags of New Zealand, Australia and all other parts of the empire; but the flag of Canada was conspicuous by its absence, and I asked a friend of mine, and in so doing, perhaps, betrayed my ignorance, why it was that the Canadian flag was not flying, and was told that we had1 no Canadian flag.
I must say that I was very much surprised the other evening at the remarks of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), an hon. gentleman who is usually very fair in his remarks and for whom I have always had a great deal of respect; I am sorry he is not in the house to-night. What he said at that time was, as reported in Hansard, at page 1959:
While assorting that we should ever aim at more and more complete independence. I say that at this time, in view of the difficult problems which are coming up in the world, in view ot the international situation which brings us the gravest problems we have ever had to solve, it is perhaps preferable that we should for the time being remain in the British commonwealth of nations. -
What are we to take from these remarks? Simply this. For all these years we have had the protection of the British flag and have enjoyed protection in the British empire, and the hon. member suggests that it would not be a good time now for us to ask for complete independence. What he means by complete independence I do not know. As the Minister of Justice pointed out, we are an autonomous nation with complete independence. Why should we remain in the British commonwealth of nations only for such length of time as we need its protection and the moment we feel we no longer need that protection sever all connection with that commonwealth?
I noted the remarks of the member for Cartier (Mr. Rose), who is not in his place to-night. I do not think that after the castigation he received this afternoon from the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) there is anything further I wish to say except this, that had he been in many another country of this world and under many another flag than the British he might have had a very serious time during these last four or . five years.
[Mr. BrooksJ
The hon. member who has just spoken referred to the graves of Canadian soldiers in different parts of France, Belgium, Holland and England. I remember during the last war when our troops were marching up through Belgium and France the people there showed respect for the union jack, as I am sure they do to-day. It was the flag which had liberated them in 1918 and which helped again to liberate their countries in 1945. I saw in windows, in stores and in houses flags which were made up of pieces of old cloth- anything the people could get hold of to represent the British flag. They also used coloured paper, which was very scarce. At any rate, they showed their respect for the British flag, the flag that had assisted in their liberation.
As was indicated in our amendment a few days ago, the Canadian ensign would be an acceptable flag for this country. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said we needed a distinctive flag. As has been pointed out, however, what more distinctive flag is there than the Canadian ensign? It has the Canadian coat of arms, representing every province in the dominion, . and in the corner the union jack, symbolizing the fact that we are a member of the British commonwealth of nations. I think it would be a most distinctive flag.
The Minister of Justice said he would not object to the maple leaf as part of the flag and I do not think there will be any serious objection in Canada. I might refer once more to the graves of our Canadian soldiers and observe that the maple leaf is the emblem which appears on practically all the crosses that mark the resting place of those men who fought and died for this country and for freedom.
May I say in closing, as a member from the maritime provinces-and I do not presume to speak for all the people of the mari-times-I am safe in saying that the great majority of the people of those three provinces would not stand for the union jack not being included as a prominent feature of our flag.

The conditions in these countries when the matter was under discussion were entirely different 47696-133
from our own. Indeed, the Australians of British extraction make up 99 per cent of the total population of their country; in Canada, it is less than 50 per cent, while the English proper make up only 25-80 per cent and the French element 30 per cent.
In this debate, we must not make the mistake of identifying the union jack with Christianity.* France is a Christian country, as are Belgium and the United States; yet, none of these countries fly the union jack.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that even though I object to our featuring the union jack on the flag, I consider myself Christian and Catholic and fully intend to remain so.

Speaking not as a French Canadian but as a Canadian, I ask that the.union jack be not featured on our flag.

The _ union jack .	.	. symbolizes British
sovereignty. When that sovereignty ceases in any dominion-that is, when the dominion itself becomes a sovereign state-further appearance of the union jack would be an anachronism and, indeed, a contradiction.

May I assure you at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that I intend to trespass upon your time and the time of this house for a matter of only five or six minutes, for I am speaking quite extemporaneously. I am moved to do so by what I thought was the very fine speech this evening of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent); and I would include also within the purview of my compliment the minister who moved the resolution. To my sorrow and perhaps my shame I was unable to find

Canadian Flag

out which side the hon. member who has just spoken was on, but no matter which side he was on I am still in favour of the resolution.
I would mention only one thing to this house, and it is this. In dealing with this question of the flag I wonder if we really conceive how far that goes. I have in mind the question of Canadian unity. It is very easy to dodge serious questions, but we gain nothing by running away from them. We all know we have had racial difficulties, and I intend to make a suggestion. I have no acrimony; I have no criticism to offer of anyone, but I think I have a constructive suggestion to make to this parliament. I had occasion to make a speech in Ottawa in 1938 I am inclined to think it was at a political convention, because I have been doing that for some time, although, in passing, I may say without very great success. On that occasion I said, and I now repeat, that it would be a sorry day for this country if the pages of our history which record the wonderful things done by the French people were ever torn out. I said that then: I meant it then, and I mean it now'. So that I am offering this broad suggestion to the house. There is onlv one way to cure this schism, this rift in our national life: that is, by all hon. members resolving something like this: That bygones are bygones. Let us not remember what somebody said in 1867 or 1877 or 1887. or anything like that. Let us take a look at this country of ours; let us be forward-looking. Therefore my suggestion is a horizontal cut-off, with no acrimony. Let us all be Canadians at heart.
I know this parliament is dealing with serious problems. We have the business of jobs; we have the business of housing, and so on; but in the long view we have nothing quite as important as the unity of the Canadian people. Jobs will be found; houses will be found, but we all have to live together for a long, long time. So that it seems to me this new parliament is in a unique position to do something. My thought is this, and I will put it in a sentence or two and leave it. We have got ourselves into a bad wav. I am not suggesting for a* moment that the faults are all on one side, because I know they are not. We have all failed; but for that reason, if for no better one, let us all resolve to do one thing. In this new parliament, with a new flag to lead us, let us begin that long and hard climb-because it will be a long and hard climb-and through the difficulties we meet and surmount as one people some day we shall reach the crest of that hill and see a new Canada, view the sunrise of a new day over

a shining, happy and prosperous land, with a people who believe in tolerance because only from tolerance comes understanding.
May I say, in closing, that as far as I am concerned, and I am sure many here will join me, I can put my position in a few words, and I use the language of San Francisco. I say that in this, to me our major undertaking, this parliament must not fail. Yea, more; in this undertaking this parliament dare not fail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I am not rising in my place to criticize the government. I wish to say just a few words about what is going on in connection with this flag issue.
Let it be understood by every hon. member that when I ask, as a member of parliament, that the house choose a flag absolutely Canadian and distinctive it is not because I am against the union jack, or any other design. Rather it is because I believe that the union jack represents another country-and that is all. I am not fighting against the union jack.
I am of French descent; yet I do not ask for the fleur-de-lis. I am asking for Canadian things. I find inspiration enough in the vast prairies of the west, in my magnificent St. Lawrence river, in the great lakes, in my Laurentides, or in the rocky mountains-in everything that is Canadian-to translate that inspiration into a flag absolutely distinct from that of any other nation. That is what I am fighting for: that is what I shall be fighting for, to the end.
Much has been said about the red ensign and about the union jack. Some have said that this was not the. proper time for the sponsoring of this resolution iby the government. Certainly, if there ever were a proper time to bring this flag issue before parliament, it is the period following the magnificent effort of Canada, the period following, as Mr. Churchill said, the amazing effort of Canada during the war. Canada must be proud enough, and all Canadians must know and believe that we are strong enough and self-conscious enough to believe and to think it is time for us to have a real, and distinctive flag.
Why all the talk about the union jack on our flag? That is the flag of the United Kingdom; it is not ours. I repeat that we do not talk about the fleur-de-lis.
If hon. members are content to listen a little longer, I would have Mr. Robert D. Mac-Lachlan of Victoria, British Columbia, speak for me. This is what he says:
At first, little if any, official attention was paid to it. However, all the while Canada was becoming more and more aware of herself. What she did and what she said finally turned the

Canadian Flag
spotlight of international surprise and admiration upon her, and at last she realized she had grown up.
Well, if we have grown up it is time for us to have a distinctive flag. He continues:
As a colony under the supreme authority and jurisdiction, of the imperial parliament, Canada's flag became the union jack (union flag). On land the union jack was flown over public buildings, and Canadian ships flew the British red ensign. However, it became necessary to make a distinction between the ships registered in Great Britain and. those registered in Canada, and the lords commissioners of the British admiralty in 1892 created a Canadian ensign which was simply a British red ensign with the Canadian coat-of-arms on the "fly". This new design proclaimed to the world that any ship flying it was a British ship registered in Canada, and sailing under the authority of the British parliament and subject to its marine laws.	.
Some have said that New Zealand has her own flag. Mr. Ewart of Ottawa who, I believe, is an authority in these matters, says this:
It is often said that New Zealand and Australia have their own national flags but this is net true. The statute of New Zealand (No. 71 of 1901) adopting its flag states: "The said ensign shall be the recognized flag of the colony-
Not of the nation.
-for general use on shore within the colony and on all vessels belonging to the colony of New Zealand or which are from time to time permitted under an admiralty warrant to use the same.
New Zealand has a colonial flag.
Someone suggested this afternoon that, to preserve unity, and to make a compromise, we should have the union jack. Is that a compromise? Do we ask for a fleur-de-lis?-and we are of French descent. You want Canada to remember that some of you are of English descent. To have that you are asking that we keep the union jack. Are we asking for the fleur-de-lis? No; we are asking for a Canadian flag.
I repeat that you should find enough inspiration in Canadian things to believe that Canada is large enough, important enough, and self-conscious enough to have her own flag, and not the flag of any other country in the world. That is what we are asking for and that is what we are going to fight for, to the end.
I hope the committee to be set up will choose a real and distinctive Canadian flag. I shall not say more, because I do not wish to prolong the debate unduly. I hope that, all being Canadians, we shall think as Canadians, and that we shall be proud enough to choose a Canadian and a distinctive flag.
I finish by saying that I hope the maple leaf will appear in a prominent place on the flag of Canada. I would refer to that song where 47696-133i
it says that we read in the maple leaf the glorious pa9t of England, that we read the admirable past of France. In Canada we love and cherish both.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, the diversity of opinion which has found expression in the house shows that the question under debate is not one of easy solution. On the other hand, the candour and courage with which these varying opinions have been put forward lead us to believe that the result of our deliberations will be a flag satisfactory to the entire population.
Three questions are raised by this resolution. The first is: is Canada to have a distinctive national flag? It is not necessary to deal with that because every one who has spoken has expressed the view for one reason o: another that it is fitting that Canada should have a distinctive national flag. The second is: is the time opportune? It seems to me it is very opportune. I am not of those who feel that our identity has been entirely blurred in the past by the fact that we had not a distinctive flag. I doubt very much if we have been confused either with our neighbours to the south, the Americans, with the people in the old land, with the Mexicans or with the people of any other nation in the concert of nations.
It is suggested that this is the proper time, and I am inclined to acquiesce in that suggestion. I think it is a very proper time because the role that Canada is being called upon to play in the international field, the expansion of our activities to many foreign lands, the establishment of legations and ministries and the like make it well that our identity should be clearly evident.
In approaching the third question, I think it might have been' better had the genius who presides over elections made a somewhat different distribution of the membership of the house. We find that all members, with seven exceptions besides myself, from my province are sitting with the government. Some may consider that a fortunate thing. In my appreciation it is unfortunate that the members of an ethnological group should find themselves all together in one political party. I say that is unfortunate, not because they are on the other side-that is a matter for them to choose-but because, did we have a certain number of that group in the party to which I belong, we would have the benefit of their counsel, the benefit of their wisdom, the benefit of their experience and consequently a better appreciation of the whole Canadian point of view.
Canadian Flag

My utterance is not made from a partisan point of view. We are dealing with a great Canadian issue, an issue that is particularly difficult to deal with because it goes into the inner life of each individual. To talk of the flag in measured language is extremely difficult because the flag is a symbol. It represents that which is personal to each citizen, to each subject, and it depicts in a way his idea of everything that is glorious in the past of his country and everything that is to be striven for in the future of his country.
It should be the attempt of this committee, when this resolution is referred to it, to find a design that will give expression to the sentiments of the whole Canadian people. The hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), who has just taken his seat, has told us his ideas. Other members have told us theirs. It is probably impossible for everyone to have exactly what he wants. The purpose or the function of parliament is to enable men to meet and hammer out their differences and find a common denominator of good will.
If the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) will permit, I will say that I thought he stated the question fairly and on a high level. He has told us candidly his personal views, his preferences and his reasons for advancing them. I for one am willing to accept his statement as the statement of an honourable and courageous gentleman. I believe that with those judicial faculties which are so highly developed in him he will be able to bring to bear upon the finding of the committee an appreciation of what is fitting and what is possible in the circumstances.
I was greatly taken the other day with one word that was uttered; by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. PearkesL He said that Canada was a nation and that a nation is a soul, a spiritual principle. To me that means two things, two things which in reality are one. The soul of a nation rests in the past as well as in the present. It is represented by a rich legacy, a rich heritage of memories from the past, and a consent, a desire even to live together in the present and' to cause that heritage recevied from the past to flourish and develop.
To have done great things together in the past, to wish to do greater things in the future seems to me to be the basis upon which must rest any idea of nationhood. Canada has achieved that greatness and to-day the eyes of the world are on Canada, not because of the extent of her territory, not because of the mileage of her railways, not because of the wealth of her mines, not even,

and we stand in awe before it, because of the bravery and sacrifice of her fighting men. The glory of Canada, Mr. Speaker, is that there has been found here a formula under which people of different origins, of different outlook and different aspirations, are able to live together in mutual respect, mutual confidence, mutual amity and1 charity. I hope that out of the committee will come a flag emblematic of that achievement, one to which the children of every citizen, whatever his background, will lift their eyes in reverence and' thanksgiving and believe that they are looking upon a banner which stands for everything of which their ancestry can be proud, no matter whence they came, and for everything for which they may hope for the prosperity and usefulness of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as I look at the motion before the house, I see that it bears the date of November 8, and to-day is November 13. This subject was mentioned in the speech from the throne, and there is no reason why the government should have waited so long to bring it before the house.
For me the question is obvious. If the committee is to meet just to ratify the choice already made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government, I wonder why the members of the committee should waste their time in sitting and looking at designs. If the thing is cooked now, why argue about the appointment of a committee? if the matter is decided, it is finished. That is my point of view. The members of the committee should be free to choose anything, and there should be no outside interference, no attempt to impose any choice upon them.
I have nothing against the union jack. I said that the other day and I repeat it to-day. In my humble view this country has not reached the stage where we should have a distinctive national flag such as is mentioned in this motion. We have not reached that time yet. We should keep the union jack, not because it is the flag of another country but because it is a flag which is the emblem of the colonialism of a certain number of Canadians in public life. They are colonials. That is why they should keep the emblem of the empire. The imperialists have no country. They are citizens without a country. Their country is the empire. They are fellow citizens of the Chinese of Asia and of the negroes of middle Africa. They are their fellow citizens. When we talk of Canada everybody is surprised. They ask: What country is it? Is it a country that is located somewhere in the sky or in another planet? The imperial-

ists are citizens of the empire; they have no country at all. The Englishman who has his domicile in the United Kingdom has a country. He has his own country, which is the United Kingdom, but the colonials who live in a colony, in a dominion like Canada, Australia, New Zealand or South Africa or any other colony pompously called a dominion, are just colonials and inferior to the British citizen who is proud of his country, the United Kingdom.

It is not at all because I am opposed to the union jack that I say that. I want to make myself clear to all the jingoes, the obtuse jingoes that we may find anywhere in this country, all those who are refractory to common sense. I tell them that so long as the flag matter is discussed with passion and sentiment it will be impossible to reach a common agreement about it.
Of course the union jack is a fine flag. It is the flag which this country should keep so long as some public men are guided by imperialism. So long as the interests of this country are not considered before those of any other country we shall have the union jack as our national flag. I say here what I have said and written elsewhere: if this country is not ripe to have her own flag let us stay as wTe are and let us keep the emblem we deserve, the emblem of colonial status; but let us not talk any more about the statute of Westminster, the autonomy of Canada and, the rank Canada has among the nations. Although I was indignant about it, Canada was called the leader of the small nations. Imagine Canada, that great country, the greatest country in the world, being the leader of the dwarf countries of the world! After what Canada has done it seems incredible. Mr. POU'LIOT: All right, ibut England owes her life to Canada and to Canadian soldiers. As Mr. Churchill and Sir John Dill have said, the only ones to defend the United Kingdom in the earlier days were the Canadian soldiers; they were the first ones to arrive. Therefore, if we owe our liberty to Great Britain, Great Britain owes her life to Canada. Let that not be forgotten.
Besides that, although it is impossible to get help for the .poor of our country we are supposed to look after those of all other countries of the world. That is the sentiment which is commonly expressed. What I deeply regret, sir, is that that noble feeling which is called patriotism is being destroyed by a new feeling which is being imposed upon us by those who have no country. It is internationalism. Internationalism is killing patriotism; and if I want a new flag, a distinctive national emblem, as it is described in the resolution, it is because I hope that parliament will decide once and for all that this country must be considered in the first place, will pass an act which is truly Canadian, and which will mean that in future Canadian public men will consider the interests of Canada before those of any other country. If we are not ready to do that, well, as has been said, let us keep the union jack. Let us be frank and sincere; let us be honest with the people. Let us keep the union jack as it is, not a minimized union jack, not a small union jack such as appears in the flag of South Africa. Let us keep the big union jack so that people will know that Canada is only a colony which makes her ''Tit-Jean Levesque" when she speaks of her importance among the nations of the world. Let us be sincere and frank about it, not hypocrites.

Mr. Speaker, I feel called upon to rise at this time to express the opinion not only of myself but of the people I represent, in saying to the members of this house that before any country adopts a flag to represent the aims, ambitions, hopes and aspirations of its people, there should be a preponderant majority in favour of that particular flag. I do not believe that we should call upon our people to look upon a flag as representing our country unless they do so with love, with pride,, yes, even with worshipful thought and meditation and profound respect.

The debates so far carried' on v in this house upon this issue do not indicate the presence of any concerted desire for one definite flag which would exemplify to a sufficient degree the feelings, the faith and the loyalty of our Canadian people. I believe that before any flag is chosen for any country it should represent the large majority of its people and embody their desires for a flag.
We have heard the viewpoints expressed here by various hon. members. Some feel that we should not supersede or in any way change the union jack as our national flag as well as the flag of our empire. Others say that the union jack should form no part of a distinctive Canadian flag. Some urge that it should constitute a prominent part of such a flag. In any event, enough has been said to indicate a very wide diversity of opinion.
Let us stop and think if this is a proper time to encourage such diversity of opinion or allow it to be accentuated in a country . which has just emerged from, a very serious war and is facing a very grave situation, and even to-night is confronted with the great strike at Windsor which is of much concern to the whole nation, and even to those beyond its borders.
Remember that our boys are still overseas, still protecting the privileges we have gained in winning the war. Let us realize that they are not home to express their views as to what kind of Canadian flag we should have.
I do not believe we shall be doing something which will inure to the unity of Canada if we attempt to put before the people a flag which does not receive the considered and almost unanimous support of the country.
I appeal to hon. members to realize that a flag, to represent Canada and all Canadians, should conform' to the ideals, hopes, ambitions and philosophy of Canadians. Let us not throw this issue into the troublesome pot now boiling over in a world which is war-torn and a nation which has still to meet difficult tasks of rehabilitation, reconstruction, social and economic reforms, and in which national unity must be established if she is to carry on the great work and occupy the great place ' in the world to which she is called.
Speaking for myself, I have not had one individual come to me and ask me to demand a Canadian national flag which shall be distinctive and different from all other flags. I have had many come to me and say, "Let us hold together; let us make progress socially; let us consider the emblem of our unity after we have gained happiness, comfort, unity and strength at home."

Canadian Flag
May I urge the members of this house to defer to some other occasion the consideration of any question that "would create difficulty or schism or ill will in these troublous days. Let us not forget that if we do send this matter to a committee that committee will consider many designs, many proposals for a new flag, and that there will perhaps be many bitter words and many thoughts expressed which may have a disintegrating effect upon our country. Then the committee will report back and the same thing will happen in this house. Perhaps to-morrow or the next day the country will be torn by a strike, or perhaps we shall find something, either in international affairs or in our own national affairs, calling for our attention, a great deal more than a distinctive Canadian national flag does.
I urge hon. members to think well before carrying on this debate to the point where we refer the matter to a committee, giving rise to still another debate in this house on the same issue. Let us postpone the question until the day when public opinion has consolidated itself into a common thought for a common design for a Canadian flag which we shall all be proud of and which we shall look upon with esteem and high regard, with reverence, yes. and even with worship. That is the kind of flag that we want, and we do not want to change the flag we have now until we have such a flag.

The hon. member said that he would prefer to leave the union jack as it is. Personally I would have no objection to leaving it as it is, although not for the same reason. I do not assume that I am colonial or that Canada, the greatest dominion in the British commonwealth of nations, is colonial. But I agree with the Minister of Justice when he says that this is an important issue and one that far transcends partisanship on either side of the house. I
have listened in this house for some years to expressions of a desire on the part of various members for a new, distinctive Canadian flag and I have seen, as you have, Mr. Speaker, some strange-coloured contraptions that were intended to represent the national character of this great young dominion.
A huncfred thousand young men have died for the flag that we have flown. Whether the Canadian ensign should have flown over these buildings I am not prepared to say. Whether that had the authority of parliament or not is a question I am not discussing. I am not so much concerned about the exact colour of the flag, but I submit that we should all be concerned at this time with what that flag represents. On other occasions private members have brought in resolutions proposing a new flag. A former member for North Battleford some years ago brought in a resolution for a distinctive flag and other private members have introduced the subject. But the government of the day, in their speech from the throne, have on this occasion brought forward the proposal for a distinctive national flag, and it is passing strange to-night to find that the senior member of the cabinet, the Minister of Justice, says that he speaks only for himself. Is there no one who can rise and speak for the government? Will my hon. friend the minister representing Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) rise and speak for the government?

May I say to those hon. gentlemen who would flirt with independence to the extent that Canada should now, when the war is over, place herself in a position of isolationism, that this country's greatness in the world is measured by the part she plays in the partnership of the British commonwealth of nations. Therefore T would say that when we decide upon the question of a national flag, and what that distinctive national flag shall be, the government should assume the responsibility, seeing especially that we are the senior dominion in the British commonwealth of nations. Let me say to those who speak of a distinctive Canadianism that I am as .proud of my Canadianism as any member of this house is of his own. and I am just as proud of Canada's achievements in this war, of Canada's place in the sun, and especially of her place in the British commonwealth of nations. I would point out to hon. members, however, that this great maritime nation should now be acting as mediator between the great regional power to the south of us and the great power of Russia in the future, and this country has a place of prominence, not in any colonial sense, but as the senior member of the British commonwealth. For these reasons, I repeat, the government should assume the responsibility in this matter. It being eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
